The runner-up is 'Not being able to stop can feel like faithfulness'. It is the counterfeit hiding inside his proudest self-image, the hard worker who came from nothing.
worst_moment: The report never reaches his children. His friend's last line is 'His kids miss him', and his eldest son is the second big question in his life. Seen and unseen came out balanced, so the one counsel written for this ('Give the people at home what strangers get') went to Andre instead. Holds firm, Enjoys comforts and 'Rest can feel like losing' are his three sharpest leanings. Together they describe his diabetes denial exactly, but no link joins them.

type_why: The Deep Well is right on the axes: serious, quiet, at her best when life is quiet. Kindred Gregory is excellent. He loved the quiet life and had the busy one forced on him, which is her dread of six weeks with her sister. Elijah checks out too (Abba Nastir in Budge). But two portrait lines get her backwards. 'People come to you when something really matters' is said to a woman who found she had no one to tell when her friend died. 'You are honest about sorrow' is said to someone who calls her long silent Sundays peace. The trap line ('being right about how badly you have been treated') aims at grievance. Her pattern is being right about how badly other people behave: the recycling bin, her sister's choices, the grandchildren's names.

links.link: You said you listen more than you talk. You also said you have whole conversations in your head that never happen.
links.why: 'An argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply.' That is her sister, her sister's husband and the building manager's inbox. It also pierces 'she believes she is tolerant'. This is the report's real aha.

links.link: You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge.
links.why: She has an opinion about what everything ought to cost, and she is sharp about her sister's choices. 'The pride of abstinence' names something she would not have put into words.

links.link: You said you fix things and move on. You also said you stop doing the wrong thing, but you are not one for saying sorry.
links.why: Her friend says she is harsher about her sister than is fair, and the sister arrives for six weeks. 'Something still needs saying' points straight at that without naming it.

links.link: You said things stay with you for a while. You also said once you are angry, it can last for days.
links.why: It is true of her, a long quiet grudge toward her sister. But it adds nothing new. It repeats the trap's moroseness quote word for word, and the anger section already says 'once it is lit, it stays lit'. It also took the fourth slot from a link that fired just as strongly and fits her better: gnat-camel (careful in small things, blind to the big one). That one describes a woman who reports a neighbour's recycling and misses her own loneliness.

fight_should_be: Sadness and Pride together, with Greed third at most. Sadness is the loneliness she calls peace. Pride is the private judging, plus 'I'd do most things better' at +2 and 'believes she is tolerant'. Sadness is a close second, which is fair. Greed leads because of how it is scored. Two prudent answers about money (think before lending, keep a little back) max out greed's leaning signal at 1.0. Pride's signal is spread over three scales, and 'Makes yourself small' zeroes one of them. A careful pensioner's thrift should not outrank the fault her friend actually sees. Vainglory as the fault that troubles her least is exactly right.
line_why: Teacher is what she picked, and it fits a retired librarian. But the kindness her friend says nobody sees is the Caregiver: soup for the old man downstairs, feeding the neighbour's cat. The report puts that second. It is defensible from her answers, but the order follows her self-image.
leanings_wrong: Having: Careful with what you have (100/100). She is precise with money, but her friend says she is 'more generous than anyone sees'. Maxing this out, then making Greed her fight and Thrift her best quality, says one thing three times. It is the one thing her friend does not flag. Self-report drove it, since every money question she answered pointed that way. Nothing asked about generosity in deeds.
Temper: Fiery (25/100). She is sharp and quick to judge, not fiery. The label also clashes with the anger section's 'It takes a lot to make you angry'.
wording_issues: 'People come to you when something really matters' is flattery that is false for her.
'You are honest about sorrow' is the reverse of her friend's view.
'Temper: Fiery' sits beside 'Hard wood. It takes a lot to make you angry.' The reader sees a contradiction.
Link 1 repeats the 'Keeps it in' card almost word for word ('The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer it').
Link 4 repeats the trap's quote ('moroseness easily slides into anger') word for word.
Money is the subject three times (top leaning, fight, best quality). It reads as one-note.

Greed card: 'a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things.' It is accurate to Gregory. But said to a woman who believes she is content, on the strength of an overweighted greed reading, it can land as harsh.

'In Christ' section: 'Your seriousness is not a flaw to be fixed. Held under reason, the fire in it becomes holy zeal.' The quote is about anger, not seriousness, so the logic jumps. It also leaves her own faith question untouched: she is moved by Bach more than sermons and wonders whether that counts.
Speaker: 'the words come hard' does not fit a retired librarian who notices misused words. She keeps her words back by choice.
'Close call: your second disposition is close' repeats itself.
best_moment: 'An argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply.' Paired with 'Your mouth needs a door, not a wall: something that opens as well as shuts', this is her friend's view in Gregory's words. Her sharpness keeps people at arm's length, and she believes she is tolerant. The door line checks out against Pastoral Rule III.14.
worst_moment: The money triple: 'Careful with what you have (100/100)', Greed as the fight, and 'Tightness can call itself good sense'. Her friend calls her more generous than anyone sees. Meanwhile the thing her friend sees first ('lonelier than she knows') is never named, and 'You are honest about sorrow' gets it backwards. Her answers said content, so self-report hid the loneliness. But quiet mind, keeps it in, makes yourself small and better in private together give enough to ask it gently.

type_why: The Spark fits the Andre on the microphone: quick, bright, hates a pause, people catch his energy. 'One more thing you enjoy a little too much' comes close to the bet without knowing it. 'You can skip past what is wrong' is him being extra cheerful at church after a big loss. But the type text is word for word Luis's. It never squares the performer with the private man, who is very hard on himself and feels a fraud. The report's own leanings show that man (Hard on yourself, Dwells on a mistake, Chooses what to show 92). 'You get things done' again sits beside 'Hard to finish (67/100)'. Augustine as kindred is apt: a young professional speaker who loved talk and pleasure and delayed giving it up. The report could have used 'not yet'.

links.link: You said you keep your disagreements with people in charge to yourself. You also said you never think your work is good enough.
links.why: He defers to his senior pastor and calls himself a humble vessel. 'Many are silent through fear, and yet consider that they are silent from humility' punctures that self-image. It is the same root as not telling Brianna. One flaw: 'never' is the report's word. He picked 'It's not good enough' as a first thought.

links.link: You said a mistake stays with you for a long time. You also said you are quick to say sorry, and sometimes do it again anyway.
links.why: This is his cycle exactly. He prays honestly, feels a fraud, and bets again, and plans to stop 'after the wedding'. 'Feeling bad is real, but it cannot do the work of changing. The sorrow is meant to lead somewhere' is the strongest line in his report. The mud image is real (Pastoral Rule III.30, on 2 Peter 2:22).

fight_should_be: Vainglory shares the lead with Greed, read as love of gain. That means chasing losses, a second credit card, and $9,000 nobody knows about. Vainglory is right: he is a performer who needs to be the one with the answers, and the Moralia speech ('aim at greater things... benefit many') fits a youth pastor perfectly. Listlessness catches the phone in staff meetings. But the one thing his friend sees him jumpy about has no place in the fight. Greed comes seventh of eight because its only private item (y3) asks about holding on to money, and the greed card itself says 'Not always wanting more'. Cassian's third kind of covetousness is the kind that makes a man 'covet and procure what he never previously possessed' (Conf. 5.11). A private item on chasing money or spending nobody knows about could reasonably have caught him. The private block is exactly where he might have admitted it.
line_why: Teacher, then Shepherd, for a youth pastor who preaches to eighty teenagers and knows every kid's little brother's name. That is right. The Caregiver (kids texting at midnight, which he picked for what people come to him for) would also have been a fair second.
leanings_wrong: Having: Open-handed (17/100). This comes from impulsive giving, but his money story is chasing losses on a hidden card. 'Open-handed' is a flattering label for a man in secret debt. The card is not shown, but the bar is.
Mood: Light-hearted (29/100). This is his self-image. His friend says something has been off lately and he is jumpy. He hides that from everyone, so self-report cannot see it.
wording_issues: The type text, 'What you bring / What it costs' and 'Your gladness is a gift' are all identical to p16's. 'You get things done' contradicts his own 'Hard to finish (67/100)'.
Link 1 says 'you never think your work is good enough'. This overstates his answer.
'Your strength: Courage... You act bravely. The risk is acting before you have thought it through.' His need is the one brave act he is avoiding, telling Brianna. Praising his courage misreads him.

'Your gladness is a gift' rings hollow for a man whose cheer is partly cover ('extra cheerful at church' after a big loss). It also leaves out what his faith section is really about: grace he can hand to others but not take for himself.

Speaks up card: the plain words steer to gossip ('idle talk slides... into talk about other people'). His speech fault is needing to have the answer and being quick to counsel. The quote itself ('no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself') fits a man who fills every pause, but the plain words do not say so.
Anger: 'Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind. Keep it that way' reads as a pat on the head. His volunteers get curtness when things are not done his way.
best_moment: 'Chooses what to show... Keeping up a guard is tiring work... Counsel: Let one person see all of you.' That answers the Brianna decision without knowing it exists. Close behind is 'The sorrow is meant to lead somewhere', which names the cycle of honest prayer and the next bet.
worst_moment: The fight never reaches the betting. It ranks Greed seventh of eight because the only greed question asks about holding on, and the greed card says 'Not always wanting more'. The private section is where he might have admitted the $9,000. In the same breath the virtue section tells him 'You act bravely'.

type_why: The disposition fits better than last round. 'You feel things deeply, and you would rather act on them than sit with them' is Ioana scrubbing the kitchen after the old man's hurtful words. 'Minds like yours find rest harder than work' is her too. The trap line ('being right about how badly you have been treated') names the resentment she is ashamed of. But the Forge's outward cast is still a fighter. The trap is labelled 'a quarrel' for a woman who never quarrels. The kindred are Chrysostom rebuking the powerful and Jerome in the thick of the fray, and she never says no to the Italian family. 'You are honest about sorrow' goes against her own leaning (Chooses what to show, 75). Her friend's central point (she lets everyone use her, and one day she will explode or fall ill) is reached only through the humility/fear lines, not through the type. The close call, The Lookout, is named with no description, so she cannot see why it might fit.

links.link: You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said.
links.why: 'The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after.' She answers the old man mildly and pays for it later. This puts into words something she has not said, and it touches her friend's fear that she will blow up one day.

links.link: You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge.
links.why: She goes without because she is building a house for her daughter. It is not self-denial for its own sake. Warning her about 'the pride of abstinence' and 'judging the undisciplined' scolds her for something nothing in her life shows. It still reads as preachy.

links.link: You said things stay with you for a while. You also said once you are angry, it can last for days.
links.why: A heavy heart feeding a slow grudge fits her resentment of the ex, her brother and the old man. But it repeats the type section's quote word for word. It also adds to a harsh self-image she already holds: she thinks she is more bitter than she is, and nothing here softens that.

links.link: You said your gut says “let me think” when a friend asks for money. You also said you find it hard to let go of money or things.
links.why: 'It is not greed for more. It is fear of less' is accurate and kindly put. For a divorced migrant with no support from her ex, it tells her what she already knows. 'Fear is answered differently from greed' is left hanging: it never says how. The second half quotes y3, one of her private answers, on the main report. The private page promises nobody sees those answers.

fight_should_be: Anger, the kind Cassian says rages inside. Anger's own speech in the report's source material ('patiently to endure them is a sin') is exactly her evening-after voice. That is the fight her friend sees: she swallows everything until she explodes or falls ill. Her private answers tie y3 (money) with y4 (replaying what someone did, +2), so the questions did catch it. Sadness, from the long separation from Daria, is close behind. Greed misreads her. 'A heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things' and 'Be content with what you need' are said to a woman who owns almost nothing. 'It is the grip, not the amount' is a real improvement, but it does not save the section.
line_why: The Caregiver is literally her life, and 'you sit with people, and you do not leave' is true. It tells her nothing new. The Watcher as her second line fits her evening prayers and the icon she kisses. The Cassian quote 'choose the care of the sick' checks out against Conference 14.
leanings_wrong: Follow-through: Hard to start (33/100). Her friend calls her the hardest-working person alive. She does everything the family asks. The one thing she 'never gets started' on is going home, and that is circumstance, not temperament.

Your mind: Holds firm (17/100). This is true of her own plans (the house). It is misleading next to her friend's view that she never says no when others push. She holds firm on her goals and gives way to demands, and the label hides the second half.

Room: Makes yourself small (92/100). This is true at work and with Italians. At the Romanian cafe she is loud, funny and bossy. Self-report could not see that. Her 'neither' on who does the talking in a group was the only hint.
help_card_wrong: 3. 'Give me time to come round. Pressure makes me dig in.' The 'dig in' gloss is the card's own addition. It is the opposite of how she meets pressure from the people she depends on: she simply takes it on. Her friend would say pressure makes her give in, not dig in.
wording_issues: 'Guard your heart after the win.' It is still unclear what 'the win' is. This was flagged last round.
'Where the trap is set for you: a quarrel.' The label does not match the text that follows ('being right about how badly you have been treated'), which describes a private grievance, not a quarrel.
'What you bring: ... You are honest about sorrow.' This contradicts her own leaning (Chooses what to show, 75) and her life: she keeps her words few.

The Moralia line 'moroseness easily slides into anger' appears twice (type and link 3). 'Silent through fear ... from humility' also appears twice (Makes yourself small, and Your best quality). The report feels padded.

'Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.' Read plainly, this is false for her. She does everything. The one true sense (she never gets round to saying no) is not stated.

'Gregory did not soften it: of the four, he calls this the worst. It is also the one where a little work changes the most.' The second sentence follows a Gregory attribution but is not his. It reads as if he said it.

'Later they remember it, and start looking for ways to get even.' The source does say 'seek reasons for vengeance', but it is harsh for a woman who scrubs the kitchen and is ashamed of her resentment.
'Gregory says grasping grows from two roots, pride and fear, and yours looks like fear.' This is a comma stack.
Link 4 quotes a private answer (y3) outside the private section.
'Held under reason, the fire in it becomes holy zeal.' This is Forge boilerplate. It fits a preacher better than a patient carer who prays the evening prayers.
'(They picked: gladly do: ... ; people come for: ...)' Debug output is still printed at the foot.
best_moment: 'Some of it may be fear that thinks it is humility ... Humility does not mean silence. Say the true thing, kindly.' Together with 'Say the hurt calmly, and soon', this is the only part that reaches what her friend Mihaela sees: she swallows everything. 'The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after' is a close second.
worst_moment: The private Greed section: 'a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things ... Be content with what you need.' It is said to a woman who has worn one coat for six years and sends almost every wage home for bricks. The 'Quick and lasting ... he calls this the worst' anger label is near it. That label confirms the bitterness she already overrates in herself, and its cure ('remember your own faults') feeds her shame instead of the counsel she needs.

type_why: 'You make hard things feel lighter. People relax around you' matches her friend's 'fun, steady'. 'A crowded week wears you down fast' fits her tired, short weeks. But 'at your best when life is quiet' is her wish, not her life. Her friend sees the glue of the hockey-parent group, the organiser who is always slightly overbooked, and the report's own line (The Shepherd: 'you organise, you take the lead') says the same. The trap ('one more helping, one more episode') paints a comfort-seeker. She is 'neither cheap nor extravagant', with one glass of wine on a Friday. St Antony, twenty years alone in the desert, is an odd kindred for the carpool organiser. It matches the Hearth template, not her.

links.link: You said you let things slide that you probably should not. You also said you calm things down when friends argue.
links.why: 'Keeping the peace can be love. It can also be the easier road.' This is her with the kids and screens, which her friend calls 'a bit soft'. Beneath it is the church question her daughter just asked, which she is letting slide. It would land harder if it linked the softness to the sudden crackdowns. She gave both answers (let things slide; snap and wish I hadn't), and the report keeps them apart.

links.link: You said people you have just met get your best. You also said you care what people think of you.
links.why: 'The people at home are the test' is a real small aha for her: the patients get cheerful Jenn and the family gets tired Jenn. The motive it supplies ('if applause is the reward') is not hers. Home gets less because she is worn out, not because she performs for praise.

fight_should_be: Listlessness, in the sense the report's own text gives it: 'Putting off the thing that matters.' Her highest private answer was y11, 'I put off the one thing that matters most' (+1). Her life says what that thing is: her daughter asked why they never go to church, and her grandmother's rosary sits unused in a drawer. Acedia's 'pious' good reasons to be elsewhere fit an always-overbooked mother. Gluttony was built from 'treat yourself' and 'enjoy a good meal' leanings plus a middling y1 (0). 'Finding it hard to stop at enough. A heavy, dull mind afterwards' describes nothing in her life or in her friend's view.
line_why: The Shepherd is exactly the hockey-parent glue: the calendar on the fridge, the carpool chat, the tournament in Sherbrooke. The Cassian example (Abbot John, a big monastery near Thmuis) checks out against Conference 14. The Host as her second line fits too. This is the part she would recognise at once.
leanings_wrong: Little things: Easy on little things (75/100). She forgets birthdays, but she runs the family calendar and the carpool group chat. Her friend sees the organiser. The label follows her answers but misses the small logistics she carries for everyone.

Make-up: Quiet mind (67/100). This is her self-image ('would like more time for herself'), not her life. Her friend describes the busy centre of a social group. Self-report could not settle this, and the report treats the wish as the fact.
wording_issues: '(Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)'. In the Pastoral Rule, Gregory gives John 16:22 ('your joy no man shall take from you') to the SAD. His word to the glad is 'Woe unto you that laugh now!' Offering the promise to the light-hearted type misapplies Gregory, even though the attribution is technically true.
'pleasure borders on mirth' is cut from a sentence where Gregory says the enemy holds out LUST as bait to cheerful people. Turning that into 'one more helping, one more episode' changes his point.
'Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace' appears twice (link 1 and the counterfeit). The peace point is made three times in all.
'Those are one thing.' This is awkward and unclear.

Kindled reeds: 'You would probably say you rarely hold a grudge. Ask someone close to you whether they agree.' This hints at grudges that nobody in her life sees. Her friend calls her steady, and she 'gets mad and gets over it'. The same sentence appears word for word in p21.
'Full in both ... You think things through.' She answered 'I sometimes say things before I've really thought them through.' The threshold leaned toward the flattering label ('worthy of praise').
'And break your own fast gladly for a guest.' This means nothing to someone who does not fast.
'(They picked: gladly do: ... ; people come for: ...)' Debug output is still printed.
best_moment: 'Keeping the peace can be love. It can also be the easier road.' It names the softness her friend sees with the kids, and quietly the church question she keeps letting slide, without scolding her.
worst_moment: 'Right now: Gluttony ... Finding it hard to stop at enough. A heavy, dull mind afterwards.' It is said to a woman whose indulgence is one Friday glass of wine and a February week in Cuba. Meanwhile her one real private admission (putting off the thing that matters most) goes unused, and it pointed straight at the faith question in her life.

type_why: The core sentence is her exactly: 'You see what could go wrong, and you would rather be doing something about it than sitting still.' That is Nadia recounting stock when frightened. 'Rest can feel like losing' is her migraine on the first day of a holiday. But the Lookout's 'careful' disposition is Gregory's 'timid', and Nadia is anxious, not timid. The timid template leaks into her report. 'What if I say it, and it costs me?' does not fit the woman who scolds old men and whose laugh turns heads across the street. 'You wait to be sure, and the moment can pass' contradicts her own answer ('decide fast and fix it later'). The kindred are Moses ('I am slow of speech') and Gideon (obeyed 'at night, because he was afraid'), both reluctant and quiet. Her friend's central point (she carries the whole street, hides her exhaustion and laughs so nobody notices) is only brushed by 'Rest can feel like losing'.

links.link: You said you let people know on the spot. You also said you snap, and wish you had not.
links.why: It mostly repeats her two answers back to her. 'The care arrives too late' is a good phrase, and it would land for a mother who snaps at her daughter. But it adds no insight. Her real pattern (taking her father's criticism in silence, then snapping at her daughter an hour later) was beyond the questions.

links.link: You said you tell people in charge when they are wrong. You also said your anger usually feels justified.
links.why: 'The feeling of being right is not proof' is a caution anyone with these two answers could receive. It roots her heat in pride. Her life, and the report's own type, say the root is fear: 'When she is frightened she gets bossy and controlling.' The quoted line is about anger mistaken for zeal and says nothing about honesty, so 'What feels like honesty can be pride' goes beyond the source.

fight_should_be: Pride is defensible, but in the form her friend sees: she 'would rather die than admit she is exhausted' and will not let anyone carry her. The report frames it as trouble taking correction and preferring her own way, which is weaker. Just as strong a candidate is Sadness of the kind the report itself describes, 'from unreasonable anxiety'. She runs disaster scenarios all night and snaps at the people she loves ('everything they say seems badly timed'). Her private y6 was 0, so self-report held it back, but her mood answers (half wait for the catch, a raised eyebrow stays all day, a criticism stays longer) pointed there.
line_why: The Giver is her shelf of medicines on credit for families who may never pay. The Advocate as her second line fits too. 'Give alms to the poor' checks out against Cassian's Conference 14.
leanings_wrong: Mood: Light-hearted (38/100). This is her self-view. Her friend says she 'worries herself sick and then makes everyone laugh so they won't notice'. The questions partly caught it: she half waits for the catch, a raised eyebrow stays with her all day, and a criticism outlasts a compliment. The average smoothed that away. This was the report's best chance at an aha, and it was missed.

Candour: Says it plainly (25/100). This is true of her opinions about others. It is false about her own state, which she hides behind jokes. Self-report cannot fully see that, and the report should not claim it.
help_card_wrong: 5. 'Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".' This comes from her 'careful' nerve score, which here is worry about disasters, not fragility under correction. She answered 'Say it straight. I can take it', 'Point out everything. I'd rather know' and 'Being told I can do better'. The round-3 rule then suppressed 'Point out everything' for her because she is 'careful'. The card goes against her own clearest answers.
wording_issues: Kindred: Moses's 'I am slow of speech and tongue' sits in the same report as 'Words first. Words come easily, sometimes before the thought is ready.' The two contradict each other.
'What if I say it, and it costs me?' and 'You wait to be sure, and the moment can pass.' These are timid-template lines that her own answers contradict.
'Gregory would call that a pair.' This puts a claim in Gregory's mouth. Better: say what he wrote.
Kindled reeds: 'Ask someone close to you whether they agree.' This is boilerplate identical to p20's, and nothing suggests she holds grudges.

'prodigality hides itself under the appellation of liberality.' The quote is real (Pastoral Rule II). She did say she gives on impulse and sometimes regrets it. But calling a pharmacist's medicine-on-credit in a collapsed economy 'scattering' may sting.

Only two links now (two were cut from round 2). Her answers held better pairs, both on her friend's view: 'I can laugh off most things' with 'I half wait for the catch', and 'I'm better off busy' with 'a week at home would wear me out'.
'(They picked: gladly do: ... ; people come for: ...)' Debug output is still printed.
best_moment: 'Gregory says the fearful should not stay in fear but grow, fed by love, until love does what fear used to do.' It is said to a woman whose faith is 'anxious and heartfelt' and who mostly bargains when she prays. This is the one line that speaks to her soul, not only her habits.
worst_moment: The kindred: Moses 'slow of speech' begging God to send someone else, and Gideon obeying 'at night, because he was afraid'. Next to 'What if I say it, and it costs me?', they are offered to the loudest, bossiest, most outspoken woman on her street. She would not recognise herself.

type_why: Cheerful, busy and energetic is fair. His life is full of routine, church duty and grandchildren, and he laughs at his own jokes. But the type's trap, pleasure ('one more helping, one more episode'), is wrong for him. He rises at five, wears a pressed shirt daily, and his own Comforts leaning says 'Keeps a tight rein'. His trap next door is pride, as every other section of the report says. Augustine as a kindred is loosely right: talk, arguments, and Augustine was a rhetoric teacher too. But the reason given is his love of pleasure, which is not Kwame at 71.

links.link: Tells people in charge they are wrong + anger feels justified: the feeling of being right is not proof
links.why: Fits the elder fighting the church building and the man who is 'stubborn about how things should be done'. The text is stock, though. The same paragraph appears word for word in p23's report.

links.link: Fixes things and moves on + not one for saying sorry: stopping does not pay the debt; something still needs saying
links.why: This is the aha. His son has never once heard him say sorry. He changes the subject with a proverb instead. The debtor image gives him the words for exactly that without calling him names.

links.link: Careful about small things + worst mistakes rare but big: straining a gnat, swallowing a camel
links.why: It fits the pressed shirts and times tables sitting beside the big unaddressed things: the son, the pride, even the roof he will not replace. It is sharp, though. It aims Christ's rebuke of the Pharisees at a church elder. It lands only because the report was gentle elsewhere.

fight_should_be: Pride first, Vainglory second, as given. His friend and son see exactly this ('never says sorry', wants his generosity known 'gently'). The 'How it shows' lines (correction hard to take, own way over advice) are him.
line_why: The Teacher, then The Giver: a retired headmaster who quizzes grandchildren and has paid school fees for a dozen children. Nothing could fit better.
leanings_wrong: Seen and unseen: balanced. His friend and family see him better in public: patient with thousands of pupils, impatient with his own son whom he corrects in front of others, and formal with his wife. He did answer that new people get his best (se1). This is the split his family most needs named, and it is flattened to 'balanced'.
Having: balanced. He paid school fees for a dozen children who aren't his. He is openly generous, and wants it known. His 'keep a little back' answer is self-image.
Nerve: balanced (42). He answered 'I can do that' at full strength, and he is described as deeply confident. Balanced understates him.
Temper: Fiery (17). He answered that anger comes slowly. His impatience is stern, lasting correction, not a flare.
help_card_wrong: 'Give me room to think out loud' asks others to feed the very habit his family endures (the 'short speech that is never short').
It leaves out his most telling answer: one person's correction he can shrug off, it takes several (he5). That is why his son's word never lands. Others could use that.
wording_issues: Pride is named in six places. The Moralia line 'so do some speak from the impatience of pride...' is quoted twice word for word (under Takes up room and again as the counterfeit). It is accurate, but it starts to read as a pile-on and a sermon.

Anger: 'Quick and lasting (only just: you sit near the middle)' is clunky. It also tells a borderline case he has what Gregory calls 'the worst' of the four, against his own answer that anger comes slowly. That is harsh on thin evidence.
'It is also the one where a little work changes the most' reads as Gregory's claim but is not shown to be his.

'How you speak' calls him 'worthy of praise' as a speaker. For a man whose speeches are never short, Gregory's warning to the talkative would be the truer word. The questions caught it (Talk 8/100, t1 at full strength).
'Takes up room: You speak up to people in charge.' He is usually the one in charge. He takes up room at family gatherings and over his son.
'You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on.' is a comma stack.
The '(They picked: gladly do: ...; people come for: ...)' line reads like a debug note, with 'They' in a second-person report.
'Gregory would call that a pair' puts a phrase in Gregory's mouth.
best_moment: 'You said you fix things and move on. You also said you stop doing the wrong thing, but you are not one for saying sorry... Something still needs saying.' His son has never heard him say sorry. This is the one true thing he has not put into words, and it is said without scolding.
worst_moment: 'Where the trap is set for you: pleasure... one more helping, one more episode.' Kwame is disciplined, and his own leaning says he keeps a tight rein. The rest of the report rightly says his trap is pride, so the type section contradicts it on the first screen.

type_why: The Hearth is right. He is mildly cheerful and likes an evening at home. He is glancing at the clock by ten at a party, and a crowded week wears him down. The pleasure trap ('one more helping') fits a man who drinks too much coffee and whose doctor wants seven kilos off. Antony the desert hermit is a grand, unrelated kindred for an ordinary Utrecht IT lead. The 'settled' point fits a little, but it is the type's stock kindred, not his.

links.link: Lets people know on the spot + snaps and wishes he hadn't: 'fury drives the mind whither desire draws it not'; the care arrives too late
links.why: True of nearly anyone who ever snaps. 'Fury' and 'the care arrives too late' overweight a man who is grumpy about cancelled trains and bikes across the gate, and whom his wife calls good company.

links.link: Tells people in charge + anger feels justified: honesty can be pride, zeal can be temper
links.why: Stock text, identical to p22's. Pieter's directness is plain Dutch manners, and he 'doesn't mind being disagreed with'. His wife sees nothing hidden and no pride. It will not land.

fight_should_be: Gluttony and Listlessness, tied, as given. The doctor's seven kilos and the coffee make Gluttony pointed and true. Cassian's 'steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts' is actually useful to him. Listlessness would be stronger if it were tied to the one thing he keeps putting off: pushing the care home about his father.
line_why: The Teacher fits an IT support lead who explains the same printer every week. The Host fits his confident weekend cooking. Both are honest to his picks. His most defining service, visiting his father twice a week though it is sad and dull, finds no voice anywhere.
leanings_wrong: Having: Careful with what you have (75). His wife and the profile say 'fairly generous': he buys a round and gives to the Red Cross. He just checks the price of cheese. 75 overstates it.
Seen and unseen: Better in private (67). His wife says 'what you see is what you get', and he answered 'neither' on se1.
Temper: Fiery (33). He is grumpy at trains, not fiery.
Little things: balanced (42). He is stubborn about small things, like how to load the dishwasher, and answered that he is careful with them.
help_card_wrong: 'Nudge me to get started' sits slightly against his answer 'Don't push. I come round in my own time' (he6). It is still broadly right given he2.
wording_issues: 'How you speak: You think things through' contradicts his own answer that he sometimes says things before thinking them through (sp2). It also contradicts the report's own 'Says it plainly' warning about truth at the wrong moment. Gregory's hasty speaker fits him better.

'Hard to start': 'people who never begin are usually busy with something else they love' does not fit him. His slowness is deliberation (two years for a phone, a year for a kitchen), and once decided it is done on schedule.

The Antony line joins two separate moments in Athanasius into one scene: the friends' amazement when he emerged after twenty years, and the cheerful face described elsewhere. It is a small liberty with a saint.
The virtue 'Glad admiration' and its counterfeit 'watching from the stands' miss what his wife names first: he is reliable. For an Ajax fan it is accidentally funny rather than true.
'Cassian's advice is steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts.' is a mild comma stack.
The pleasure-trap sentence and the whole type paragraph are word for word the same as p24's.
best_moment: 'Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.' That is the man who took two years to change phones and is now weighing whether to push his father's care home.
worst_moment: The stock pair 'What feels like honesty can be pride.' It is aimed at a plain-spoken man who doesn't mind being disagreed with and whose wife says nothing is hidden. He would shrug, and it costs the report credibility.

type_why: Light-hearted and fond of comfort is right: the nap with the TV on, the vetkoek, hymns in the car. 'At your best when life is quiet' and 'a crowded week wears you down fast' are her tired self-view. Her friend calls her 'the person you want beside you in a crisis'. She enjoys parties, the catch-up after a funeral and the savings club braai. A self-report quiz can't easily see past fatigue. Still, the type describes her rest, not her strength. Antony, twenty years alone in the desert, is a poor kindred for a woman whose faith is 'communal and sung'.

links.link: Lets things slide she shouldn't + calms things down when friends argue: 'Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace'
links.why: This matches what Lindiwe sees: too soft with relatives who ask for money. It also matches the irritation with latecomers she voices only to Lindiwe. 'It can also be the easier road' is fair. The word 'sloth' may sting a woman up at 4:45, but it is Gregory's word, and the report softens it.

links.link: People just met get her best + cares what people think: 'Those are one thing'; applause as reward; the people at home are the test
links.why: It joins two separate answers and gives her a motive, applause-seeking, that nothing in her life shows. Her giving is private and goes to family. She irons uniforms at 4:45 and raises her late sister's son. The only true kernel is that she sometimes snaps at home, and the anger section already covers that.

fight_should_be: Gluttony is defensible from her own answers: comfort food when low, snacks, and high blood pressure. Anger, the evening snapping, is rightly second. Her real overreach, giving past her means, is not one of the eight. It is rightly handled under Open-handed rather than forced into Greed, which correctly sits low.
line_why: The Caregiver, then The Giver. 'You sit with people, and you do not leave' is exactly Lindiwe's 'the person you want beside you in a crisis'. Giver is the relatives and the bride-price loan.
leanings_wrong: Make-up: Quiet mind (71). This is her fatigue talking. Her friend sees steadiness under pressure, and her life is sociable and full.
Candour: balanced. She keeps her irritations to herself except with Lindiwe, which leans towards 'Chooses what to show'.
Nerve: Careful (63). She is described as steady and neither anxious nor carefree. 63 overstates caution.
help_card_wrong: Only one line ('Tell me in private'), thin beside the others. Her answers offered more: 'Ask for my help' (he7), 'Pick the one thing that matters most' (he4), 'Show me someone doing it' (he1).
wording_issues: 'Simply glad': 'Admiring is not the same as trying... If you admire it, try it', with 'inert spectators'. Said to a working mother raising three children and a grieving nephew, this is unfair. The same 'eager backers, but inert spectators' quote appears again as her counterfeit.
'The fault is never in the food. It is in the wanting' appears twice, under Enjoys comforts and again in the fight section.
'Those are one thing.' is an odd sentence, and it asserts a link the answers do not support.
Open-handed counsel 'do not keep score' misses her risk. She doesn't keep score. She skips her own hair appointment and can't say no. The Gregory warning about giving so much you run short does fit.
Her virtue, 'Glad admiration', misses what her friend names: steadiness and staying with people in a crisis. The report's own Caregiver line says it better.
The type paragraph is identical to p23's, word for word.
'You serve by staying close when things are hard. You sit with people, and you do not leave.' is good. The Teacher-style comma stack does not appear here.
best_moment: 'The Caregiver... You sit with people, and you do not leave.' Beside it is the Open-handed warning about giving so much you run short, which fits the skipped hair appointment. Together they say what Lindiwe says.
worst_moment: 'If applause is the reward, Gregory says, you are selling it cheap. The people at home are the test.' It gives a vanity motive to a woman whose generosity goes quietly to family. Together with 'if you admire it, try it', it is the one place the report is unfair to her.
